content: 1. The Quantiferon-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT-GIT) test, an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) endorsed by the World Health Organization (WHO), is being phased out by its manufacturers and replaced with the Quantiferon-TB Gold Plus, a four-tube test. 2. Updated laboratory request forms, registers, and laboratory information systems must be supplied to document and report IGRA test results effectively. 3. Additional funding considerations for implementing TB testing programs include the cost per test, the estimated number of target populations for testing, and logistical support for individuals undergoing testing and healthcare workers accessing tuberculin skin tests (TST) and IGRA testing. 4. Incentives for healthcare workers and laboratory technicians, maintenance of the cold chain for tuberculin, and ongoing training and capacity building are essential for program success. 5. Laboratory services for IGRA testing, specimen collection, and transport must be maintained, and additional laboratory technicians may need to be hired, including from the private sector. 6. Strengthening supply chain management is critical to ensure an uninterrupted supply of tuberculin, IGRA blood collection tubes, and reagents. 7. Tools for routine data capture, preferably electronic, should be implemented to streamline operations. 8. The tuberculin skin test (TST) has advantages such as being field-performable, requiring fewer resources compared to IGRA, and not needing a laboratory setup. It is familiar to practitioners in resource-limited settings and can provide results within 24 hours without a booster effect or false positives due to BCG vaccination. 9. Challenges with TST include the need for training in intradermal injection and interpretation, a second visit for test reading, global shortages of purified protein derivative (PPD), cold chain requirements, and higher costs compared to IGRA. 10. IGRA testing requires sophisticated laboratory equipment, skilled personnel, and phlebotomy, with potential delays in sample transport and processing. Results may take at least one day, and batching tests to reduce costs can further delay reporting. 11. IGRA is preferred for children under two years of age, settings with poor laboratory infrastructure, and individuals unlikely to return for TST reading, such as homeless persons or those with job constraints. 12. WHO recommends shorter, safer, and more affordable TB preventive treatment (TPT) regimens, urging governments and donors to support access to these regimens. 13. TPT regimens fall into two categories: six or nine months of daily isoniazid monotherapy or shorter rifamycin-based regimens, assuming the infecting strain is susceptible to these drugs. 14. Isoniazid preventive treatment (IPT) for six months has been widely used and remains a standard for TPT in both high and low TB incidence countries. However, shorter rifamycin-based regimens are increasingly recommended due to better adherence and fewer adverse events. 15. WHO recommends several TPT options, including six or nine months of daily isoniazid, three months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, three months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin, one month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid, or four months of daily rifampicin alone. 16. The choice of TPT regimen should consider factors such as age, drug susceptibility, risk of toxicity, availability, and patient preferences. Shorter regimens are preferred for better adherence and completion rates. 17. For children under five years of age, the three-month daily isoniazid plus rifampicin (3HR) regimen is better tolerated and more child-friendly due to the availability of dispersible fixed-dose combination (FDC) formulations. 18. Rifapentine-containing regimens, such as three-month weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP) or one-month daily isoniazid plus rifapentine (1HP), are effective alternatives but require further data for dosing in children under 12 years of age. 19. Four-month daily rifampicin (4R) is a cost-effective option with an excellent safety profile, particularly for contacts of individuals with isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible TB. However, concerns about rifampicin resistance and drug-drug interactions with antiretrovirals must be addressed. 20. National programs should weigh factors such as country context, health system capacity, and resource availability when selecting TPT regimens. Efforts to scale up shorter regimens are likely to improve adherence and completion rates. 21. The 2020 WHO guidelines broaden the applicability of TPT regimens across all TB burden settings, emphasizing the importance of reliable TB disease exclusion, proper implementation, and measures to limit TB infection and reinfection risks. 22. Isoniazid remains the preferred regimen for HIV-infected children on protease inhibitor-based regimens or integrase inhibitors due to potential drug-drug interactions with rifamycin-based regimens. 23. The availability of rifapentine at discounted prices and the anticipated introduction of FDC tablets combining rifapentine and isoniazid will reduce the pill burden for patients prescribed 3HP. 24. Preventive treatment for pediatric TB is strategically important due to the increased risk of progression to severe TB forms in young children. Delivering TPT effectively can avert pediatric TB and its complications.
